message_text:
Real hope, real change — that’s what a fairer, greener Britain looks like. I strongly support a joined-up set of policies that put people and planet first. We must urgently accelerate renewable energy — more offshore and onshore wind and community solar — so power is cheap, clean and owned by us, not distant shareholders. That means banning new oil, gas and coal licences, because expanding fossil fuel extraction locks in higher bills and ever-worsening climate harms.

To make the transition tangible in everyday life, I strongly back banning the sale of new petrol cars by 2030 and ensuring every new home is built with non-fossil fuel heating, rooftop solar and top-level insulation. Warmer, low-cost homes and electric transport cut bills and emissions together. To ensure fairness, we should impose a carbon tax on fossil fuel sales and return the revenue to households through a fee-and-dividend — protecting low-income families while sending a clear market signal to polluters.

Finally, we must show international solidarity by compensating people in other countries who are already suffering from climate impacts we helped cause. This package is cohesive: public renewables and home retrofits lower bills; a phase-out of fossil licences and a carbon dividend make polluters pay; global compensation reflects our responsibility. For the common good — fairer, greener communities and a secure future for everyone.

Listen — we all want a safe future for our kids, but this Westminster-greenprint is not a plan, it’s a price-rise dressed up as virtue-signalling. I strongly oppose rushing headlong into a package that accelerates offshore and onshore wind farms, bans new oil and gas licences, and forces a 2030 ban on petrol car sales. I oppose mandates forcing every new home to have non‑fossil heating, rooftop solar and costly insulation standards. I oppose a new carbon tax — even if they promise a “dividend” — and I oppose sending our cash abroad to compensate other countries for climate impacts.

Why? Because these policies stack costs on ordinary working families, pensioners and small businesses already crushed by sky-high energy bills. More turbines, fewer domestic oil and gas licences and a petrol ban won’t lower prices quickly — they’ll hand power to foreign grids and leave our industries cold. Mandates on housing and electric cars will push up house prices, commuting costs and local taxes. A carbon tax is just another stealth bill; giving the proceeds back as a token “dividend” won’t cover higher bills. And shipping taxpayer money overseas while our own communities suffer is backwards patriotism.

We should scrap these ideological diktats, reopen realistic home-grown energy production, cut green levies, and back British workers and farmers instead of pursuing Net Zero at the expense of prosperity. Scrap Net Zero to cut energy bills — restore Britain’s power and prosperity.

Real hope, real change — that’s the future I want to fight for. I strongly support a joined-up programme that puts people and planet first: rapidly accelerating renewable energy, banning new oil, gas and coal licences, ending sales of new petrol cars by 2030, mandating non-fossil heating, rooftop solar and top-level insulation on new homes, introducing a carbon fee-and-dividend, and compensating communities abroad harmed by the climate emergency.

Why these measures together? Because they break the grip of profit-driven polluters while making life fairer and cheaper for ordinary families. More offshore and onshore wind and clean power means secure, local jobs and the cheapest electricity we’ve ever had. Stopping new fossil licences and phasing out petrol cars ends the false choice between jobs and the climate — we can have both through investment in renewables and public transport. Requiring green heat, solar and insulation in new housing brings warm homes and lower bills from day one. A carbon fee-and-dividend ensures polluters pay, while returning revenue to households protects low-income families as prices shift. And as a wealthy nation, we must help communities overseas already suffering the climate impacts we helped cause.

This is not radical — it’s practical stewardship. For the common good: fairer, greener communities that secure a safe future for everyone.

I’m broadly in favour of speeding up renewables — wind and solar make sense and can cut bills, though I want real community ownership and biodiversity safeguards. I slightly support banning new oil/gas/coal licences as a signal, but only if it’s paired with clear plans to protect workers and energy security. I slightly support a 2030 ban on new petrol car sales — it’s the right direction but feels tight unless we massively improve public transport and help lower‑income households access EVs. I slightly support requiring new homes to have non‑fossil heating, rooftop solar and high insulation, provided affordability and social housing aren’t left behind. I’m ambivalent about a carbon fee‑and‑dividend: I like the principle of making polluters pay and returning revenue to people, but I’d need strong evidence the dividend protects the worst off and that industry can’t evade responsibility. I slightly support compensating people in other countries hit by climate change on moral grounds, though I’m wary about how payments would be administered and whether they tackle root causes.

I broadly support accelerating renewables — cheaper local clean power and jobs make sense — but I’m cautious about onshore siting, community consent and any hit to household bills. I’m conflicted about banning new fossil licences and a strict 2030 petrol‑car ban: I accept the direction but want phased, well‑funded transitions and proper infrastructure so families aren’t left worse off. I’m mixed on mandating green standards for new homes (good long‑term, worry about upfront costs), mildly supportive of a fee‑and‑dividend carbon tax (the dividend helps fairness), and only mildly comfortable with large international compensation unless it’s transparent, limited and clearly tied to outcomes.

I broadly support speeding up renewables like wind, but only if sites are chosen carefully with proper environmental assessments and real community consultation here in Wales. I lean towards banning new oil/gas/coal licences in principle, though I want a well‑managed transition that protects jobs and local economies rather than a sudden ban. I support a 2030 ban on new petrol cars in principle because it’s important for emissions, but I worry about affordability for ordinary families and rural charging infrastructure. I’m broadly in favour of requiring new homes to have non‑fossil heating, rooftop solar and high insulation — it makes sense long‑term — provided there are subsidies or exemptions so first‑time buyers aren’t priced out. I’m mildly supportive of a carbon fee‑and‑dividend because the dividend protects lower‑income households, but I’m unsure if revenues might be better spent on insulation, rural infrastructure and worker transition programs. I also think we should help people overseas hit by climate change out of moral duty, though I’d want transparent, accountable mechanisms to ensure the aid actually reaches those in need.

Real hope, real change — that’s what a fairer, greener Britain looks like. I strongly support a joined-up package of policies that puts people and planet first: rapidly accelerating renewable energy like offshore and onshore wind, banning new oil, gas and coal licences, and ending the sale of new petrol cars by 2030. These steps are not about sacrifice; they’re about common-sense investment that lowers household bills, creates local jobs, and gives young people a secure future.

Building genuinely sustainable communities means mandating non-fossil heating, rooftop solar and high levels of insulation on all new homes. Insulation is the single biggest bill-buster we have — warm homes, lower bills, and lower emissions. To ensure the transition is fair, I strongly support a carbon fee-and-dividend: taxing fossil fuel sales and returning the revenues to the public so the cost falls least on those who can’t afford it.

The climate emergency is global and our responsibilities are too. I strongly support compensating people in other countries already harmed by climate change — it’s about justice and international solidarity. Together, these policies form a coherent plan: public action that curbs corporate profits from pollution, funds a green transition, and delivers fairer, greener communities for everyone. For the common good.

I oppose this whole package of climate dogma. Ordinary hard-working families are already crushed by energy bills and punished by endless Westminster virtue-signalling — and this plan would make it worse. Ramming through an accelerated wind roll-out and banning new oil and gas licences will hand our energy security to expensive, intermittent power and force us to import more power and minerals from overseas. Banning petrol cars by 2030 and forcing every new house to have non-fossil heating, rooftop solar and top-tier insulation is a one-size-fits-all diktat that slams working people and small businesses with upfront costs while enriching installers, consultants and the same global green industry that hardly pays UK taxes.

A carbon tax paid back as a “dividend” is just another hidden bill: families will still see higher prices at the pump and in their heating bills, and bureaucrats will decide who gets what. And using British taxpayers to compensate people in other countries for climate impacts turns our hard-earned cash into a foreign aid cheque for elites’ conscience.

We should scrap this ideology-driven assault and put British households first: get real about protecting jobs, cut green levies from bills, back sensible domestic energy production in the North Sea, and stop treating the countryside and drivers as enemies. Net Zero as policy is Net Poverty for Britain.

I’m broadly in favour of faster deployment of renewables like wind because it actually cuts emissions and can bring local jobs, but I worry projects must be sited with proper biodiversity safeguards and genuine community ownership. I slightly support banning new oil/gas/coal licences as a signal of transition, though only if it comes with managed plans for workers and energy security. I slightly support a 2030 ban on new petrol car sales—ambitious and helpful for decarbonising transport, but it risks being unfair without big subsidies, a strong used‑EV market and much better public transport. I slightly support mandating non‑fossil heating, rooftop solar and high insulation for new homes, provided there’s support for social housing and small builders so it doesn’t push up costs. I’m ambivalent about a carbon fee‑and‑dividend: I like the idea of returning revenues to people, but I’m sceptical about whether the design would be truly equitable or more effective than strong regulation. I slightly support compensating people in other countries harmed by climate change on moral grounds, but I’d want clear, accountable mechanisms to ensure aid reaches those who truly need it and addresses long‑term resilience, not just one‑off payouts.

Requiring new homes to have non‑fossil heating, solar and good insulation appeals to me — it seems sensible and could cut bills long term, provided developers don’t just pass costs onto buyers or renters. I broadly support the package — I’m especially keen on accelerating renewables and making new homes energy-efficient because they promise local jobs, long-term bill savings and help the environment. I strongly oppose this whole package of climate policies — it isn’t a sensible plan, it’s an out‑of‑touch ideological crusade that slams ordinary Brits for the benefit of the Westminster Green Blob.

First, accelerating wind parks and banning new oil and gas licences will jack up bills and hand more power to foreign supply chains while crippling our North Sea industry and the jobs that go with it. Banning petrol cars by 2030 and forcing every new house to install non‑fossil heating, rooftop solar and top‑tier insulation sounds virtuous in Whitehall briefing rooms, but for hard‑working families and small builders it’s a ruinous cost and an assault on personal freedom—another stealth tax on motorists and homeowners.

A carbon tax with a dividend dressed as fairness still drives up energy and fuel prices, squeezing wages and killing businesses; handing back a cheque doesn’t undo the damage of higher heating and transport costs. And spending UK cash to compensate people abroad? We should help in genuine emergencies, not funnel British taxpayers’ money to satisfy guilt-driven global schemes while our own communities suffer.

We need common-sense energy policy that puts Britain’s workers, farmers and drivers first: scrap these ideological mandates, restore North Sea production, cut green levies, and stop bankrupting the country in the name of Net Zero. Net Zero is Net Poverty — and ordinary people won’t pay for elite virtue signalling.

Real hope, real change: we urgently need a joined-up plan that tackles the climate and cost-of-living crises together. I strongly support accelerating renewable energy — more offshore and onshore wind and community solar — because cheap, locally owned clean power cuts bills and keeps money in our towns, not in shareholders’ pockets. That’s why I strongly back banning new oil, gas and coal licences: continuing to hand out licences to polluters is the reason bills and emissions stay high.

I strongly support a ban on the sale of new petrol and diesel cars by 2030, paired with free or affordable public transport for young people and investment in charging and active travel. Homes are at the heart of this recovery, so I strongly support mandating non‑fossil heating, rooftop solar and high insulation in all new developments — warm homes, lower bills and far fewer emissions.

To make polluters pay and people benefit, I strongly support a carbon fee-and-dividend: taxing fossil fuels fairly and returning revenues to households so families are protected while we move to clean energy. And crucially, I strongly support compensating communities abroad harmed by climate change — global solidarity is part of a fair transition.

This is about a secure future for everyone: public ownership, wealth re-invested in our communities, and policies that deliver fairer, greener communities now.

That’s why I strongly back banning new oil, gas and coal licences: continuing to hand out licences to polluters is the reason bills and emissions stay high.

I strongly support a ban on the sale of new petrol and diesel cars by 2030, paired with free or affordable public transport for young people and investment in charging and active travel. Homes are at the heart of this recovery, so I strongly support mandating non‑fossil heating, rooftop solar and high insulation in all new developments — warm homes, lower bills and far fewer emissions.

To make polluters pay and people benefit, I strongly support a carbon fee-and-dividend: taxing fossil fuels fairly and returning revenues to households so families are protected while we move to clean energy. And crucially, I strongly support compensating communities abroad harmed by climate change — global solidarity is part of a fair transition.

This is about a secure future for everyone: public ownership, wealth re-invested in our communities, and policies that deliver fairer, greener communities now.

Real hope, real change: we must act now to protect people and planet. I strongly support an urgent, joined-up plan to accelerate renewable energy — more offshore and onshore wind, community solar and storage — because cheap, clean power is the foundation of fairer bills and local jobs. That means immediately banning new oil, gas and coal licences so we stop underwriting the industries that keep prices and emissions high, and legislate to end sales of new petrol cars by 2030 so our streets are cleaner and transport is affordable and electric for everyone.

I strongly back requiring every new home to be built with non‑fossil heating, rooftop solar and high levels of insulation. Warm, efficient homes cut bills, reduce demand for energy and create skilled local retrofit jobs. To ensure a just transition, I strongly support a carbon fee-and-dividend: tax fossil fuels at source and return the revenues to households, protecting low‑income families while sending a clear market signal to polluters.

Climate breakdown is global, so I strongly support compensating countries and communities already suffering its impacts — moral duty and practical solidarity. Together these policies form a single vision: public-first energy, secure homes and shared prosperity. For the common good — fairer, greener communities and a secure future for everyone.

That means immediately banning new oil, gas and coal licences so we stop underwriting the industries that keep prices and emissions high, and legislate to end sales of new petrol cars by 2030 so our streets are cleaner and transport is affordable and electric for everyone.

I strongly back requiring every new home to be built with non‑fossil heating, rooftop solar and high levels of insulation. Warm, efficient homes cut bills, reduce demand for energy and create skilled local retrofit jobs. To ensure a just transition, I strongly support a carbon fee-and-dividend: tax fossil fuels at source and return the revenues to households, protecting low‑income families while sending a clear market signal to polluters.

Climate breakdown is global, so I strongly support compensating countries and communities already suffering its impacts — moral duty and practical solidarity. Together these policies form a single vision: public-first energy, secure homes and shared prosperity. For the common good — fairer, greener communities and a secure future for everyone.

I strongly oppose this whole package of climate grand-standing dressed up as “progress.” Forcing more offshore and onshore wind parks and banning new oil, gas and coal licences will slam ordinary families and British industry with higher energy costs and less reliable power. Telling people they can’t buy petrol cars after 2030 and forcing non-fossil heating, rooftop solar and extreme insulation on every new home is another layer of hidden taxes and red tape that hits working people hardest — motorists, tradesmen, farmers and small businesses who rely on cheap, dependable energy and transport to make a living.

A carbon tax with a so-called “dividend” is still a penalty on families and firms: levies get hidden in bills and prices, and the state grows fatter while households get poorer. And why should Britain be writing blank cheques to compensate people overseas for climate impacts when our own towns are losing manufacturing, our farmers are under siege, and energy bills are at crisis levels?

This isn’t environmental care — it’s an elite Net Zero crusade that sacrifices livelihoods for virtue-signalling targets. Scrap these ideological mandates. Keep Britain’s energy affordable and secure, back our drivers and farmers, and stop taxing people into poverty in the name of climate dogma. Restore common-sense energy policy that puts jobs and families first.

Real hope, real change: we strongly support a joined-up plan that puts people and planet first. It’s time to accelerate renewable energy — vastly more offshore and onshore wind and community-owned solar — so that cheap, clean power is the backbone of our economy, not a profit engine for privatised giants. That means banning new oil, gas and coal licences now, because continuing to open the door to fossil fuel extraction triples down on the same system that drives bills up and heats the planet.

This is about building fairer, greener communities where the common good comes first — a secure future for everyone.

I generally like the package — I’m especially positive about accelerating renewables and tightening new‑build standards because they cut emissions, can lower bills and create local jobs, though I want genuine community ownership and strong biodiversity safeguards. I slightly support bans on new fossil licences and a 2030 petrol‑car sales cutoff as urgent signals, but both need properly funded worker/community transitions, big support for low‑income and rural households (scrappage, charging, public transport) and a healthy used‑EV market to be fair. I’m ambivalent about fee‑and‑dividend and overseas compensation: principled in theory, but I’d only back them if there are clear, transparent designs and governance to prevent regressivity or capture and ensure funds actually reach the people and places that need them.

Homes are where lives — and bills — are made or broken. Together, these policies form a single, fair vision: public control of energy, homes that cost less to run, and a green transition funded by those who created the crisis — for the common good and a secure future for everyone.

To make polluters pay and people prosper, I strongly support a carbon fee-and-dividend: tax fossil fuels and return the revenues to households to protect low-income families while driving the low-carbon transition. And because climate justice must be international, I strongly support compensating people in other countries suffering climate impacts — solidarity and fairness are essential.

Together, these policies form a single, fair vision: public control of energy, homes that cost less to run, and a green transition funded by those who created the crisis — for the common good and a secure future for everyone.

Real hope, real change — that’s the kind of bold, practical government I passionately support. We urgently need to accelerate renewable energy: build more offshore and onshore wind and community-owned solar so power is cheap, clean and controlled by the people, not profiteers. That’s why I strongly support banning any new oil, gas or coal licences — fossil fuels have no place in our future and every new licence locks in higher bills and hotter summers. To speed the shift on our roads, I strongly support a 2030 ban on new petrol car sales, paired with affordable electric alternatives and free public transport for young people so no one is left behind.

I strongly oppose this whole package of Net Zero diktats. It’s not clever policy; it’s an ideological sledgehammer being brought down on ordinary people who can’t afford it. Forcing through a rapid roll-out of wind farms and slapping bans on new oil, gas and coal licences will send energy bills through the roof, wreck jobs in our North Sea industry and hand control of our power to unpredictable weather and foreign supply chains. Banning new petrol cars by 2030 is a direct tax on working families, farmers and small businesses who rely on vehicles to do their jobs — it’s urban nannying shoved down the throat of the rest of the country. Requiring every new home to be fitted with non-fossil heating, rooftop solar and top-end insulation is another construction cost hike which will be paid by first-time buyers and renters. A carbon tax with rebates sounds nice on paper, but it simply entrenches the “green levy” model that inflates bills and fuels inflation. And while compassion for people harmed by extreme weather abroad is understandable, diverting scarce resources to international compensation while Britons struggle to heat their homes is the wrong priority. Scrap these costly mandates. Restore British energy common sense: back domestic production, cut green levies, and stop imposing elite climate projects that make the many poorer to appease the Westminster bubble.

I’d broadly support a faster roll‑out of renewables — especially if projects are community‑owned, protect biodiversity and deliver local jobs rather than being imposed top‑down. I slightly support a ban on new oil/gas/coal licences as a strong signal against lock‑in, but only if it’s part of a properly funded, managed transition for workers and energy security plans. I slightly support a 2030 ban on new petrol car sales because decarbonising transport matters, though that deadline feels tight and needs big scrappage schemes, rural charging and better public transport to avoid unfair harm. I slightly support mandates for non‑fossil heating, rooftop solar and high insulation in new homes — it makes long‑term sense for bills and emissions, but must include protections so affordable housing and small builders aren’t squeezed. I’m ambivalent about a carbon fee‑and‑dividend: the dividend idea is promising for fairness, but I’m sceptical about design and governance and would need clear, transparent rules to be convinced it wouldn’t be regressive or captured. I slightly support compensating people in other countries harmed by climate impacts on moral and practical grounds, provided there are robust, accountable delivery mechanisms so the money actually helps those most vulnerable.

I’m only mildly supportive of international compensation in principle; I’m sympathetic to helping those hit hardest, but I’d need robust, transparent delivery and governance guarantees before fully backing big overseas payments.
